                                 EL PASO ELECTRIC COMPANY
                                 REBUTTAL TESTIMONY OF
                                    OMAR A. GALLEGOS

 1                  I.    INTRODUCTION AND QUALIFICATIONS

 2   Q1.   PLEASE STATE YOUR NAME AND BUSINESS ADDRESS.

 3   A.    My name is Omar A. Gallegos. My business address is 100 N. Stanton Street,

 4         El Paso, Texas, 79901.

 5

 6   Q2.   BY WHOM AND IN WHAT CAPACITY ARE YOU EMPLOYED?

 7   A.    I am employed by El Paso Electric Company ("EPE" or the "Company") as

 8         Vice President of Energy Delivery.

 9

10   Q3.   HAVE YOU PREVIOUSLY SUBMITTED TESTIMONY IN THIS CASE?

11   A.    Yes. I submitted Direct Testimony on August 6, 2026, in support of EPE’s

12         Amended Application for Revision of its Retail Electric Rates (“Amended Filing”).

13

14   Q4.   ARE YOU SPONSORING ANY EXHIBITS IN THIS FILING?

15   A.    No.

16

17                  II.    PURPOSE OF REBUTTAL TESTIMONY

18   Q5.   WHAT IS THE PURPOSE OF YOUR REBUTTAL TESTIMONY?

19   A.    My rebuttal testimony has three purposes. First, I respond to Coalition for Clean

20         Affordable Energy (“CCAE”) witness Ron Nelson’s direct testimony on EPE’s



                                                1
                                   EL PASO ELECTRIC COMPANY
                                   REBUTTAL TESTIMONY OF
                                      OMAR A. GALLEGOS

 1         proposed revisions to the line extension policy for large load customers, including

 2         Mr. Nelson’s categorization of connection and transmission upgrades into

 3         customer-specific, dedicated upgrades and “but for” upgrades, and his concerns that

 4         EPE’s revised policy does not adequately address shared “but for” transmission

 5         costs to fully protect existing ratepayers from cost shifts.

 6                 Second, I respond to the direct testimony of New Mexico Public Regulation

 7         Commission Utility Division Staff (“Staff”) witness Orland Whitney on meter-

 8         exchange safety concerns with customer owned facilities.

 9                 Third, I address Staff’s Witness Mr. Bunch’s concerns and recommendations

10         on EPE’s Rate No. 11. On this point, my testimony addresses: (1) the purpose and

11         presentation of lumen and wattage information in the tariff; (2) the use of LED

12         wattage ranges and cost-based rates; (3) EPE's selection and installation of LED

13         luminaires in relation to roadway-lighting criteria; (4) Staff's proposed photometric

14         study; (5) conversion of mercury-vapor and high-pressure-sodium lighting to LED;

15         (6) customer-requested conversion charges; (7) vicinity conversions; and (8) Staff's

16         proposed unified lighting tariff.

17

18                         III.     LINE EXTENSION POLICY

19   Q6.   CCAE WITNESS MR. NELSON CATEGORIZES CONNECTION AND

20         TRANSMISSION UPGRADE COSTS TRIGGERED BY LARGE LOAD



                                                  2
                                  EL PASO ELECTRIC COMPANY
                                  REBUTTAL TESTIMONY OF
                                     OMAR A. GALLEGOS

 1         CUSTOMERS INTO TWO TYPES OF UPGRADES - “CUSTOMER-

 2         SPECIFIC, DEDICATED UPGRADES AND “BUT FOR UPGRADES.” DO

 3         YOU AGREE?

 4   A.    Partially, I agree there are customer specific upgrades. I do not agree with his

 5         definition of “but for upgrades” and his recommended treatment. I address this

 6         further in rebuttal testimony.

 7

 8   Q7.   DO YOU HAVE ANY COMMENTS ON MR. NELSON’S EXPLANATION

 9         OF “DEDICATED” FACILITIES AND “BUT FOR” FACILITIES ON

10         PAGES 44 TO 45 OF HIS DIRECT TESTIMONY?

11   A.    EPE’s definition of dedicated facilities are those that only serve the specific

12         customer. This could be a substation fully dedicated to serving that customer, a

13         substation transformer or distribution feeder fully dedication to only serving that

14         customer. A transmission line that is radial only serving that customer may also be

15         dedicated. On the contrary, it is important to highlight that what he refers to as

16         “but for” facilities become shared network facilities. For this reason, the treatment

17         should be handled differently. EPE witness Mr. Novela addresses EPE’s treatment

18         for these shared network upgrades triggered by a large load customer.

19




                                                 3
                                  EL PASO ELECTRIC COMPANY
                                  REBUTTAL TESTIMONY OF
                                     OMAR A. GALLEGOS

 1   Q8.   WHAT IS MR. NELSON’S ASSESSMENT OF EPE’S PROPOSED LINE

 2         EXTENSION POLICY TREATMENT OF DEDICATED FACILITIES

 3         SERVING LARGE LOADS?

 4   A.    Mr. Nelson agrees with EPE’s proposal to assign costs to large load customers for

 5         any dedicated facilities via a customer specific facility charge, which he

 6         characterizes as a “step in the right direction.” However, he expresses concern that

 7         EPE’s proposed policy does not go far enough to ensure customers provide security

 8         or certainly not to walk away and cover their obligation.

 9

10   Q9.   DID MR. NELSON PROPOSE REVISIONS TO THE POLICY TO

11         ADDRESS THIS?

12   A.    Mr. Nelson recommends that EPE provide “more detail on several aspects of the

13         proposal,” to address three areas: (1)      limited information on formula and

14         methodology used for the proposed Infrastructure Capacity Charge and

15         determination of payment period and cost recovery guarantees as compared to other

16         charges; (2) allowing Infrastructure Capacity Charge to be paid overtime creates

17         ongoing ratepayer exposure if the customer exists service before full recovery; and

18         (3) the Company has not defined what qualifies as an “unplanned substation

19         upgrade.”

20



                                                4
                                EL PASO ELECTRIC COMPANY
                                REBUTTAL TESTIMONY OF
                                   OMAR A. GALLEGOS

 1   Q10. DO YOU AGREE WITH MR. NELSON’S CONCERN THAT EPE DOES

 2        NOT     ADDRESS       SUFFICIENT       REQUIREMENTS           TO    PROTECT

 3        ONGOING RATEPAYER EXPOSURE IF A LARGE LOAD CUSTOMER

 4        EXITS?

 5   A.   No. Mr. Nelson fails to recognize that large load customers above 10 MW of load

 6        are categorized into NM Rate 51 (or NM Rate 50 if they are a high load factor

 7        customer with demand above 30 MW). EPE witness Manny Carrasco describes

 8        both NM Rate 50 and 51 in his Direct Testimony and were filed as Exhibits MC-

 9        09 and MC-10. Both NM Rate 50 and 51 have provisions for minimum monthly

10        bill for a term of twenty years. Furthermore, the tariffs require minimum credit

11        worthiness or security requirements to protect other customers from stranded

12        infrastructure investments.

13

14   Q11. DOES       THIS      PROTECT        CUSTOMERS          FROM        STRANDED

15        INVESTMENTS IF LARGE LOAD CUSTOMER CEASE OPERATING OR

16        LEAVE?

17   A.   Yes.

18

19   Q12. WHAT IS YOUR RESPONSE TO MR. NELSON’S RECOMMENDATION

20        ON DEFINING AN “UNPLANNED SUBSTATION”?



                                             5
                                  EL PASO ELECTRIC COMPANY
                                  REBUTTAL TESTIMONY OF
                                     OMAR A. GALLEGOS

 1   A.   The EPE reference to an unplanned substation refers to a substation not identified in

 2        its Ten-Year Distribution System Plan. If it is in the Ten-Year Distribution System

 3        Plan it would be an acceleration. However, treatment is also on a case-by-case basis if

 4        the accelerated substation for the customer will be a dedicated customer facility or a

 5        subset of the substation capacity. EPE requires flexibility to assess the specifics for

 6        treatment of facilities with the distinguishing fact being if a dedicated facility. The

 7        proposed line extension allows for flexibility for varying customer interconnections

 8        that may arise.

 9

10   Q13. HOW DO YOU RESPOND TO MR. NELSON’S CONCERN THAT EPE

11        DOES      NOT      PREDEFINE          TREATMENT         OF     FACILITIES        AND

12        CALCULATIONS FOR FACILITIES CHARGES?

13   A.   Each customer interconnection and infrastructure requirements will be unique to each

14        interconnection. Therefore, assessment of customer dedicated facilities versus those

15        that are network upgrades would be assessed on a case-by-case basis. Any customers

16        with a load above 10 MW will be assigned to Rate 51 which defines minimum bill

17        requirements and security requirements. The negotiated Energy Service Agreement

18        will define the facilities charge and term.

19

20   Q14. WHAT IS MR. NELSONS ASSESSMENT OF EPE’S PROPOSED LINE



                                                  6
                                 EL PASO ELECTRIC COMPANY
                                 REBUTTAL TESTIMONY OF
                                    OMAR A. GALLEGOS

 1        EXTENSION POLICY TREATMENT OF “BUT FOR” FACILITIES?

 2   A.   Mr. Nelson is concerned that EPE’s revised policy would not directly allocate

 3        shared, “but for” facilities. Mr. Nelson recommends that facilities that are triggered

 4        because of a large load customer should be fully paid for by the large load customer.

 5

 6   Q15. DO YOU AGREE WITH MR. NELSON ON THIS PREMISE?

 7   A.   No. The need for the facilities may have been triggered by the large load customer

 8        but are part of the transmission network that serves all customers. EPE witness

 9        George Novela addresses Mr. Nelson’s recommendations to require advanced

10        payment of “but for” transmission upgrades through a CIAC with refunding

11        mechanism and explains how rate making and customer class allocation would be

12        addressed in a future rate case proceeding subsequent to facilities being placed into

13        service.

14

15                               IV.    METER SAFETY

16   Q16. WHAT IS STAFF WITNESS ORLAND WHITNEY’S SAFETY CONCERN

17        RELATED TO THE METER EXHANGE FROM LEGACY METERS TO

18        ADVANCED METERING SYSTEM?

19   A.   Mr. Whitney raises a safety concern that unsafe or deficient condition of other

20        components of a service installation can prevent safe installation or re-energization



                                                7
                                 EL PASO ELECTRIC COMPANY
                                 REBUTTAL TESTIMONY OF
                                    OMAR A. GALLEGOS

 1        even when a meter replacement is sound. To address this concern, Mr. Whitney

 2        asked EPE to provide rebuttal addressing its meter-exchange procedures and how

 3        that safety concern is addressed.

 4

 5   Q17. DOES EPE HAVE METER-EXCHANGE PROCEDURES TO ADDRESS

 6        UNSAFE        OR      DEFICIENT             CUSTOMER-OWNED         EQUIPMENT

 7        IDENTIFIED         DURING        A      METER     EXCHANGE,         INCLUDING

 8        CUSTOMER NOTIFICATION, CORRECTIVE ACTION, SERVICE DE-

 9        ENERGIZATION OR RECONNECTION?

10   A.   Yes. EPE has established practices for identifying and addressing unsafe or

11        deficient conditions during a meter exchange. Safety takes precedence when

12        performing this work, and the action taken by EPE personnel depends upon the

13        severity of the condition identified.

14               EPE owns and is responsible for the electric meter. The meter enclosure or

15        meter socket, including the components within the enclosure, is customer-owned

16        equipment. Service equipment located on the customer's side of the meter enclosure

17        is also customer-owned and is the customer's responsibility to maintain and repair.

18               When an EPE employee identifies a deficiency involving customer-owned

19        equipment, the employee evaluates the condition to determine whether it presents

20        an imminent safety hazard. If the condition does not present an imminent safety



                                                  8
                                EL PASO ELECTRIC COMPANY
                                REBUTTAL TESTIMONY OF
                                   OMAR A. GALLEGOS

 1       hazard, the employee red tags the service, providing the customer 10 days to correct

 2       the identified deficiency. When possible, the EPE employee attempts to contact the

 3       customer directly and explain the condition. If the customer is not available, the

 4       employee leaves a door hanger notifying the customer that the service has been red

 5       tagged, identifying the reason for the red tag, and explaining the corrective action

 6       required.

 7              If the condition presents an imminent safety hazard, EPE takes immediate

 8       action to protect the customer, EPE personnel, and the electric system. The

 9       customer is notified of the unsafe condition and the service is de-energized.

10       Because the deficient meter enclosure or associated service equipment is customer-

11       owned, the customer is responsible for completing the necessary repairs. Service

12       may be re-energized after the required corrections have been completed and the

13       installation is in a condition that permits EPE to safely provide service.

14              EPE's procedures establish a clear and consistent process: EPE evaluates

15       the safety condition, notifies the customer, identifies the required corrective action,

16       and responds according to the severity of the condition; the customer is responsible

17       for repairing customer-owned equipment; and EPE proceeds with the meter

18       exchange or restores service once the installation can be safely energized.

19

20   Q18. DO EPE’S METER-EXCHANGE SAFETY PROCEEDURES APPLY TO



                                               9
                                 EL PASO ELECTRIC COMPANY
                                 REBUTTAL TESTIMONY OF
                                    OMAR A. GALLEGOS

 1        BOTH CUSTOMERS WITH AMS AND NON-AMS METERS?

 2   A.   Yes. This procedure is consistently applied regardless of whether the customer

 3        currently has an AMS meter or a non-AMS meter. EPE's response is based on the

 4        condition and safety of the customer-owned equipment, not the type of meter

 5        installed at the premises. Accordingly, the identification of an unsafe or deficient

 6        meter enclosure does not create a separate safety process for an AMS customer or

 7        a customer with a non-AMS meter.

 8

 9                              V.     STREET LIGHTING

10   Q19. PLEASE      SUMMARIZE           STAFF      WITNESS       BUNCH'S        PRINCIPAL

11        RECOMMENDATIONS RELATED TO LIGHTING.

12   A.   Mr. Bunch recommends that EPE revise Rate No. 11 to remove or correct lumen

13        information, establish narrower 10-watt ranges for Company-owned LED lights,

14        revise conversion language and evaluate a marginal-cost approach for customer-

15        requested LED conversions, and evaluate broader changes to EPE's street-lighting

16        practices. He also recommends field photometric testing, an analysis of vicinity

17        conversions, and consideration of a unified tariff for different lighting technologies.

18

19   Q20. DO YOU AGREE WITH THE PRINCIPAL RECOMMENDATIONS?

20   A.   I do not agree that the record supports those broad directives, although EPE can



                                                10
                                   EL PASO ELECTRIC COMPANY
                                   REBUTTAL TESTIMONY OF
                                      OMAR A. GALLEGOS

 1        clarify outdated or potentially confusing tariff language as part of an orderly tariff

 2        update.

 3

 4   Q21. DO YOU AGREE THAT THE LED LUMEN INFORMATION IN RATE NO.

 5        11 INDICATES THAT EPE IS PROVIDING INADEQUATE OR

 6        EXCESSIVE ROADWAY ILLUMINATION?

 7   A.   No. The tariff is a rate schedule, not a site-specific photometric design document.

 8        A comparison between the nominal lumen rating of a legacy high-pressure-sodium

 9        lamp and the delivered output of an LED luminaire does not, by itself, establish the

10        amount or distribution of light reaching a roadway. LED performance depends on

11        the complete luminaire, including its optical system and distribution pattern, as well

12        as mounting height, pole spacing, roadway geometry, surface conditions, and the

13        lighting criteria applicable to the location. Accordingly, the different lumen values

14        cited by Mr. Bunch do not establish that an installed LED fails to provide

15        appropriate lighting.

16

17   Q22. SHOULD         EPE       NEVERTHELESS             CLARIFY         THE       LUMEN

18        INFORMATION SHOWN IN RATE NO. 11?

19   A.   Yes. EPE can clarify the tariff, so customers do not read legacy lumen figures as

20        the actual rated output of every LED luminaire within a tariff category. A



                                                11
                                 EL PASO ELECTRIC COMPANY
                                 REBUTTAL TESTIMONY OF
                                    OMAR A. GALLEGOS

 1        reasonable update would accurately identify the column as a service-equivalency

 2        designation, replace the figures with verified fixture information, or remove the

 3        column if it is not needed to administer the rate. This limited clarification does not

 4        establish that EPE's installed lights are noncompliant or unsafe. (See rebuttal

 5        testimony of Rene Gonzalez.)

 6

 7   Q23. DO THE EXISTING COMPANY-OWNED LED WATTAGE RANGES

 8        DEMONSTRATE THAT EPE'S STREET-LIGHTING RATES ARE NOT

 9        COST BASED?

10   A.   No. A rate category does not have to reproduce the exact cost of each individual

11        luminaire model. Street-lighting cost of service includes more than energy use. It

12        may include the installed luminaire, poles and associated facilities, maintenance,

13        service work, labor, transportation, inventory, administration, and other costs

14        assigned to the service. Reasonable rate design commonly groups equipment with

15        similar service characteristics to create rates that are understandable and practical

16        to administer. The fact that two LED models have different wattages or purchase

17        prices does not, standing alone, establish that a grouped rate is unreasonable.

18

19   Q24. IS STAFF'S COMPARISON TO THE PROPOSED CUSTOMER-OWNED

20        LED WATTAGE RANGES PERSUASIVE?



                                               12
                                  EL PASO ELECTRIC COMPANY
                                  REBUTTAL TESTIMONY OF
                                     OMAR A. GALLEGOS

 1   A.   No. Customer-owned and Company-owned lighting services recover different

 2        bundles of service and are not interchangeable. For Company-owned lighting, EPE

 3        owns and maintains the facilities and the rate may recover capital investment,

 4        maintenance, replacement, service labor, transportation, inventory, administration,

 5        and energy. For entity-owned lighting, the entity owns and maintains the facilities

 6        after construction and EPE generally charges for the energy service provided. A

 7        narrower wattage structure for entity-owned service therefore does not establish

 8        that the same structure is required for Company-owned service. Any change to

 9        Company-owned ranges should be based on EPE's underlying cost-of-service and

10        billing data, not solely on the shape of another tariff table.

11

12   Q25. SHOULD THE COMMISSION ORDER EPE TO CREATE 10-WATT

13        COMPANY-OWNED LED RATE BANDS WITHIN THREE MONTHS?

14   A.   No. That deadline would require a rate-design change before the associated costs,

15        billing impacts, customer migration, and tariff administration are fully evaluated.

16        If the commission determines that additional Company-owned LED categories are

17        warranted, the change should be supported by cost data and implemented through

18        the appropriate tariff and rate-review process.

19

20   Q26. CAN THE RANGE OF WATTAGES IN A TARIFF CATEGORY



                                                13
                                 EL PASO ELECTRIC COMPANY
                                 REBUTTAL TESTIMONY OF
                                    OMAR A. GALLEGOS

 1        ESTABLISH THAT EPE HAS NOT FOLLOWED ROADWAY-LIGHTING

 2        CRITERIA WHEN REPLACING HID LUMINAIRES?

 3   A.   No. Mr. Bunch infers field noncompliance from tariff categories. That inference

 4        conflates rate classification with design selection. A wattage band used for billing

 5        does not direct field personnel to install any luminaire in that band at any location

 6        without regard to conditions. Luminaire selection is a design and operational

 7        decision that considers the location, fixture type, optical distribution, mounting

 8        configuration, roadway characteristics, and the lighting objective. A broad tariff

 9        range therefore does not establish that the installed equipment departs from

10        applicable roadway-lighting criteria.

11

12   Q27. HOW DOES EPE USE ANSI/IES RP-8-25 ROADWAY-LIGHTING

13        GUIDANCE IN SELECTING LED LUMINAIRES?

14   A.   EPE in general practice uses applicable design criteria and fixture-specific

15        manufacturer photometric information when selecting LED street-lighting

16        equipment. The selection is made through coordination between EPE Engineering

17        Standards and the Lighting Department, with consideration of the installation

18        location, roadway or area characteristics, mounting configuration, optical

19        distribution, pole spacing, and the intended lighting objective. RP-8-25 guidance

20        evaluates performance at the roadway or area being illuminated; it does not require



                                                  14
                                EL PASO ELECTRIC COMPANY
                                REBUTTAL TESTIMONY OF
                                   OMAR A. GALLEGOS

 1        an LED luminaire to reproduce the source-lumen rating of the outgoing HID lamp.

 2        The relevant inquiry is whether the selected luminaire and installation are

 3        appropriate for the location and intended service, not whether two technologies

 4        have identical published lumen values.

 5

 6   Q28. DOES THE ABSENCE OF A FIELD PHOTOMETRIC SURVEY FOR

 7        EVERY CONVERSION ESTABLISH A SAFETY PROBLEM?

 8   A.   No. Field measurements are one tool, but they are not the only method for

 9        evaluating a luminaire. Manufacturer photometric files, design layouts, equipment

10        specifications, visual   inspections, customer reports, and targeted field

11        measurements can all inform lighting decisions. Field readings can also vary with

12        pavement condition, weather, surrounding light, vegetation, pole condition,

13        voltage, and measurement method. Staff has not identified specific installation,

14        measurement, accident analysis, or other field evidence to indicate EPE's LED

15        conversions created a systemic safety problem.

16

17   Q29. SHOULD THE COMMISSION ORDER THE BROAD FIELD STUDY

18        PROPOSED BY MR. BUNCH?

19   A.   I believe a more focused study would be appropriate. EPE would be willing to

20        conduct a focused review of existing LED roadway-lighting installations, done by



                                             15
                                 EL PASO ELECTRIC COMPANY
                                 REBUTTAL TESTIMONY OF
                                    OMAR A. GALLEGOS

 1        EPE, in New Mexico. However, roadway lighting represents a limited portion of

 2        EPE’s current lighting activity in New Mexico, with most involving private-area

 3        lighting. For that reason, I believe the scope of any study should be proportionate

 4        to the number and type of roadway-lighting installations that remain in service.

 5

 6   Q30. DO YOU AGREE THAT RATE NO. 11 CONTAINS LEGACY LANGUAGE

 7        REGARDING          MERCURY-VAPOR              TO    HIGH-PRESSURE-SODIUM

 8        CONVERSION?

 9   A.   Yes. To the extent the tariff refers to replacing mercury-vapor lighting with high-

10        pressure-sodium lighting, that language should be reviewed and updated to reflect

11        equipment currently available and EPE's present practices. Updating legacy

12        language is a reasonable tariff clarification. It does not mean, however, that every

13        remaining HID luminaire must be converted immediately or that all conversion

14        costs should be shifted to other customers.

15

16   Q31. DOES EPE CURRENTLY INSTALL NEW MERCURY-VAPOR OR HIGH-

17        PRESSURE-SODIUM LUMINAIRES?

18   A.   EPE's current practice is to use LED equipment for all new street-light installations

19        and for replacements when the applicable luminaire is no longer serviceable.

20



                                               16
                                EL PASO ELECTRIC COMPANY
                                REBUTTAL TESTIMONY OF
                                   OMAR A. GALLEGOS

 1   Q32. SHOULD RATE NO. 11 EXPLAIN THAT A CUSTOMER MAY REQUEST

 2        AN ACCELERATED CONVERSION FROM HID TO LED?

 3   A.   EPE does not oppose a limited tariff clarification stating that a customer may

 4        request an accelerated conversion. However, all requests must be evaluated based

 5        on ownership, equipment condition, remaining investment, engineering

 6        requirements, scheduling, materials, and the work required at the location. A

 7        voluntary early conversion is different from replacing failed or unavailable

 8        equipment in the ordinary course. Rate No. 11 should preserve EPE's ability to

 9        recover the incremental and unrecovered costs caused by a customer's decision to

10        accelerate replacement.

11

12   Q33. DO YOU AGREE WITH STAFF'S PROPOSED MARGINAL-COST

13        FORMULA FOR CUSTOMER-REQUESTED GROUP CONVERSIONS?

14   A.   Not as proposed. Planned group conversions may create efficiencies, but comparing

15        those conversions with EPE’s normal reactive replacement approach requires

16        consideration of EPE-specific factors such as equipment condition, expected

17        replacement timing, location, crew and material requirements, and remaining

18        investment. EPE can evaluate these costs and potential savings for a customer-

19        requested group conversion, but the analysis should not assume a predetermined

20        conversion date such as 2032. Any resulting charge should reflect the actual costs



                                              17
                                 EL PASO ELECTRIC COMPANY
                                 REBUTTAL TESTIMONY OF
                                    OMAR A. GALLEGOS

 1        and savings of the project and avoid shifting costs to other customers.

 2

 3   Q34. WHAT IS THE APPROPRIATE COST-RECOVERY PRINCIPLE FOR A

 4        CUSTOMER-REQUESTED EARLY CONVERSION?

 5   A.   The requesting customer should be responsible for the costs that EPE would not

 6        otherwise incur at that time. This includes applicable costs for removal, installation,

 7        engineering, transportation, labor, and any unrecovered investment attributable to

 8        retiring serviceable equipment, subject to the approved tariff. EPE may evaluate a

 9        coordinated group project when it creates demonstrable savings, but any credit for

10        avoided future costs should be supported by EPE-specific data and should not

11        create a subsidy from nonparticipating customers.

12

13   Q35. DO YOU AGREE WITH STAFF'S RECOMMENDATION THAT COSTS

14        TO REMEDY ALLEGEDLY NONCOMPLIANT LED INSTALLATIONS

15        SHOULD BE EXCLUDED FROM RATE BASE OR O&M EXPENSE?

16   A.   No. I do not believe such a determination can be made based on the information

17        presented. The wattage ranges shown in the tariff do not, on their own, establish

18        that an EPE LED installation is inconsistent with applicable roadway-lighting

19        criteria. Any future corrective work and associated cost recovery should be

20        evaluated on the specific circumstances, supporting engineering information, and



                                                18
                                 EL PASO ELECTRIC COMPANY
                                 REBUTTAL TESTIMONY OF
                                    OMAR A. GALLEGOS

 1        applicable ratemaking standards.

 2

 3   Q36. SHOULD THE COMMISSION ORDER EPE TO COMPLETE STAFF'S

 4        PROPOSED VICINITY-CONVERSION STUDY WITHIN SIX MONTHS?

 5   A.   No. Coordinated conversions may make sense in certain areas, and EPE can

 6        evaluate those opportunities as they arise. The decision depends on the number and

 7        condition of remaining HID luminaires, customer needs, engineering requirements,

 8        crew and material availability, traffic control, and overall cost. This approach

 9        allows EPE to pursue conversions where they are practical and beneficial while

10        maintaining flexibility to respond to street-light outages efficiently

11

12   Q37. DOES EPE OPPOSE EVALUATING PLANNED GROUP CONVERSIONS

13        WHERE CIRCUMSTANCES SUPPORT THEM?

14   A.   No. Planned group conversions may be appropriate when multiple HID luminaires

15        are concentrated in an area, the customer requests or supports the project,

16        engineering review is complete, materials and traffic-control needs are planned, and

17        the project produces verifiable savings. However, EPE should retain discretion to

18        evaluate those opportunities using EPE-specific operational and cost data rather

19        than being required to complete a study on a predetermined schedule or adopt

20        Staff's assumed method.



                                                19
                                 EL PASO ELECTRIC COMPANY
                                 REBUTTAL TESTIMONY OF
                                    OMAR A. GALLEGOS

 1

 2   Q38. DO YOU AGREE WITH STAFF'S PROPOSAL FOR A UNIFIED TARIFF

 3        COVERING MV, HPS, AND LED LIGHTING?

 4   A.   No. A unified rate can obscure real differences in investment, energy usage,

 5        maintenance, remaining book value, and service obligations among technologies

 6        and equipment configurations. Charging the same rate merely because two lights

 7        are described as functionally equivalent can shift costs among customers and

 8        weaken cost causation. Technology-specific or service-specific rates remain more

 9        transparent while different equipment and costs remain on the system.

10

11   Q39. IS THE TIMING OF AN INDIVIDUAL LUMINAIRE CONVERSION

12        ALONE       A    SUFFICIENT         REASON       TO     DISREGARD         COST

13        DIFFERENCES?
